newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open softer, dollar still strong.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open softer, dollar still strong.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened narrowly lower on Tuesday, mildly pressured by profit-taking after a run-up a day earlier, analysts said.
"There's some profit-taking but the flows have been pretty two-way," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.

Renewed dollar strength gave Treasuries a bit of a bid in Tokyo, Rupert said, but those gains were lost during London trade as the dollar strength was offset by weaker euro-government debt markets, she said.
Rupert pointed to some pressure on the market from the launching of a $1.0 billion five-year eurobond deal.

Dollar strength could give Treasury prices a lift, as it did on Monday, she said. The dollar was strong in early U.S. dealings, just below a 51-month peak of 126.52 yen reached in Europe. It was also firm against the mark.
But Rupert said trading in Treasuries was likely to be narrow-ranged.
"I don't expect to see the kinds of gains we saw yesterday," she said.

The market faces a limited calendar of economic data on Tuesday. The Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi index of chain store sales, officially released at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, is rumored to be down 0.8 percent for the week ending April 5.
Another privately collected index of retail store results for the week ended April 5, the Redbook report, is due at 1455 EDT/1800 GMT.

The government will release February wholesale inventory figures at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. According to a Reuters poll, economists estimate inventories rose 0.4 percent in February after January's 1.0 percent gain.

The wholesale inventory data are not expected to move the market. For potentially market moving government economic data, the market has to wait to the end of the week -- to Thursday's weekly report on new and continuing jobless claims and to Friday's reports on producer prices and retail sales.

According to a Reuters poll, the March Producer Price Index (PPI) is forecast at unchanged after falling 0.4 percent in February. Retail sales are forecast to be up 0.6 percent after a 0.8-percent February gain. Analysts said the PPI is important, but carries a little less weight for the market than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) due next wee.
Retail sales will be looked at with great interest because monetary policy maker are focused on the demand side of the economy and consumers are responsible for about two-thirds of that demand.
The market will also pay attention to remarks that Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern makes in a keynote address at a Minneapolis Fed community conference at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
In early trade on Tuesday, three- and six-month bill rates were each down one basis point to 5.09 percent and 5.30 percent, respectively.
Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.62 percent.

Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.40 percent. In other key issues, the five-year note was down 1/32 to 99-19/32 to yield 6.72 percent, and the 10-year was down 3/32 to 95-20/32 to yield 6.87 percent.
The benchmark 30-year bond was down 6/32 to 94-10/32, yielding 7.08 percent.
